chapter: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
question_text: Describe the tissue culture technique. What are the advantages of tissue culture over the conventional method of plant breeding in crop improvement programmes?

steps.label: What tissue culture is
steps.margin_note: Definition, totipotency, and all six steps listed. This opening is worth a mark by itself.
lines: TISSUE CULTURE is the technique of growing,
culturing and maintaining cells, tissues and
organs IN VITRO — in glass, outside the plant.
It is based on the property of TOTIPOTENCY: the
ability of any living plant cell to regenerate
into a complete plant.
The six steps of the technique are:
1. prepare the medium  2. sterilise it
3. prepare the explant 4. inoculate
5. incubate for growth 6. acclimatise and
transfer to pots.
steps.why: Totipotency is what makes the whole technique possible: without it a fragment of tissue could never become a whole plant.
common_mistakes: Leaving out totipotency. It is the principle the technique rests on.
Saying tissue culture works only on seeds. ANY living plant part can be used.
Naming fewer than six steps. Six is what the book gives and six is what the marks follow.
steps.memory_tip: Any living cell can rebuild the whole plant: that is totipotency.

steps.label: Medium and sterilisation
steps.margin_note: Every component of the medium, then the three autoclave figures.
lines: 1. PREPARATION OF THE NUTRIENT
MEDIUM The medium must supply a CARBON
SOURCE such as SUCROSE, inorganic salts, vitamins,
amino acids, and growth regulators such as AUXINS and
CYTOKININS.
2. STERILISATION OF THE MEDIUM
A nutrient rich medium attracts micro organisms,
so it must be sterilised.
Sterilisation is done in an AUTOCLAVE for 15
minutes at 121°C and 15 lb pressure.
steps.why: The medium is a perfect food for bacteria and fungi as well as for the plant tissue, so anything not sterilised will be overgrown before the explant can start.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the autoclave figures. 15 minutes, 121°C and 15 lb are the numbers asked for.
Saying the medium contains glucose. The carbon source given is SUCROSE.
Forgetting the growth regulators. Auxins and cytokinins are part of the medium.
steps.memory_tip: Rich food feeds the contaminants too, so sterilise everything.

steps.label: Explant and inoculation
steps.margin_note: Define explant, give examples, and name the laminar air flow chamber.
lines: 3. PREPARATION OF THE EXPLANT
Any living part of a plant used as the inoculum
is called an EXPLANT — a piece of root, stem,
leaf or a shoot tip.
The explant is surface sterilised.
4. INOCULATION OF THE EXPLANT
Transferring the explant onto the sterile medium
is called INOCULATION.
It is carried out in a LAMINAR AIR FLOW
CHAMBER, which supplies filtered, sterile air.
steps.why: Every transfer is a chance for contamination, so the one step where the culture is open to the air is done under a filtered air stream.
common_mistakes: Not defining explant. It is a named term and often asked alone.
Leaving out the laminar air flow chamber. It is where inoculation must happen.
Saying the explant is sterilised in the autoclave. It is SURFACE sterilised; an autoclave would kill it.
steps.memory_tip: The explant is the piece you start from, and it goes in under sterile air.

steps.label: Incubation and callus
steps.margin_note: The time, the divisions, and the definition of callus.
lines: 5. INCUBATION FOR GROWTH
The cultures are incubated for 3 to 4 WEEKS.
During this time the explant cells absorb
nutrients, grow, and divide repeatedly by
MITOSIS.
They produce an UNDIFFERENTIATED mass of
cells called the CALLUS.
steps.why: The callus is undifferentiated on purpose: a mass of unspecialised cells can be pushed down any developmental path by changing the hormones.
common_mistakes: Saying the callus is differentiated tissue. It is an UNDIFFERENTIATED mass.
Leaving out the time. Three to four weeks is the figure given.
steps.memory_tip: A shapeless lump of cells that can still become anything.

steps.label: Organogenesis and embryogenesis
steps.margin_note: Both paths named and distinguished, plus artificial seeds.
lines: From the callus there are TWO paths:
(i) ORGANOGENESIS: adding AUXINS and
CYTOKININS to the medium induces the callus to
produce ORGANS — roots and shoots.
(ii) EMBRYOGENESIS: the explant may develop an
embryonic callus, from which EMBRYOIDS are
produced.
Because these embryoids develop from SOMATIC
(body) tissue and not from gametes, they are
called SOMATIC EMBRYOS.
Somatic embryos can be coated to make ARTIFICIAL
SEEDS.
steps.why: Which path the callus takes depends only on the balance of hormones in the medium, so one callus can be steered either way.
common_mistakes: Confusing the two paths. ORGANOGENESIS gives organs; EMBRYOGENESIS gives embryoids.
Saying somatic embryos come from gametes. They come from SOMATIC tissue — that is what the name means.
Leaving out artificial seeds. They are the practical product of somatic embryos.
steps.memory_tip: Somatic means body: these embryos had no gametes.

steps.label: Acclimatisation
steps.margin_note: The gradual transfer and the reason. This is the last step of the technique half.
lines: 6. ACCLIMATISATION AND TRANSFER TO
POTS Plants raised in culture have grown in warm,
humid, sterile conditions and are not ready for
the open field.
They are HARDENED OFF gradually — first in a
glass house, then in pots, then in the field.
Without acclimatisation the plantlets die when
they are transferred.
steps.why: A plantlet grown in a sealed tube has a thin cuticle and few functioning stomata, so it would dry out at once in open air.
common_mistakes: Transferring straight to the field. The plantlets must be hardened off first.
Leaving out the reason. The plantlets die without it, and that is why the step exists.
steps.memory_tip: A plant raised in a jar cannot survive a field on its first day.

steps.label: Diagram — the tissue culture flow chart
steps.margin_note: No diagram mark. Draw it if you have time: it is the fastest way to check all six steps are in your answer and in the right order.

elements.text: 3. Take the explant from a plant

elements.caption: Step 3 — the callus takes one of two paths
Step 4 — both paths give plantlets, then a field crop

elements.text: 6. Harden off, then to the field

steps.why: The flow chart shows what a list of six steps hides: the two paths out of the callus rejoin, so both organogenesis and embryogenesis end in plantlets.
common_mistakes: Drawing one path out of the callus. There are TWO, and they rejoin at the plantlet stage.
Putting sterilisation after inoculation. The medium is sterilised BEFORE the explant goes in.
Ending at 'plantlets'. Acclimatisation and transfer to the field are the last box.
steps.memory_tip: One chain, one fork, one merge, one field.

steps.label: Advantages
steps.margin_note: Two marks. At least five numbered advantages, each with its reason. Do not let the technique half eat the time this half needs.

lines.text: Fast, virus free, identical, and it works

lines: ADVANTAGES OF TISSUE CULTURE OVER
CONVENTIONAL
BREEDING:
1. Many more plants can be produced in a SHORT
TIME and in a small space
(MICROPROPAGATION).
2. VIRUS FREE plants can be raised from SHOOT
TIP cultures, because meristems are free of virus.
3. SEEDLESS plants can be multiplied, which
sexual reproduction cannot do at all.
4. FEMALE plants can be produced selectively.
5. SOMATIC HYBRIDS can be raised where sexual
hybridisation is impossible.
6. Medicinal plants can be cultured to yield
high value products of industrial and medicinal
importance.
7. The plants produced are SOMACLONES —
genetically identical to the parent.
steps.why: Each advantage comes from the same fact: tissue culture bypasses sexual reproduction entirely, so it is not limited by what can be crossed with what.
common_mistakes: Giving fewer than five advantages. Two marks need a real list.
Saying tissue culture produces variation. It produces SOMACLONES — genetically IDENTICAL plants.
Leaving out virus free plants. It is the advantage examiners ask about separately.
steps.memory_tip: No sex means no limits on what can be multiplied.
